title: "PCE Components"
---

```{R}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
library(zoo)
library(psych)
library(kableExtra)
```

FRED-QD, the McCracken-Ng quarterly companion to FRED-MD, includes national-accounts series that only exist at quarterly resolution. We use three components of real personal consumption expenditures (PCE):

- `PCDGx`: durable goods (autos, appliances, furniture)
- `PCNDx`: nondurable goods (food, energy, clothing)
- `PCESVx`: services (healthcare, housing, recreation)

These three sum to total PCE (`PCECC96`), so some correlation is built in by construction. But they behave very differently. Durables are big-ticket, credit-sensitive purchases people postpone in a downturn and catch up on later — the most cyclical of the three. Nondurables are closer to necessities, smoother but not immune to recessions. Services are the smoothest of all in normal times — healthcare and rent don't swing with the business cycle — except in 2020, when lockdowns hit services spending directly and produced the sharpest quarterly move in this entire dataset.

Dates run `r format(as.Date("1959-06-01"))` through `r format(as.Date("2026-06-01"))`.

```{R pce-load-data-levels}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| label: pce-load-data-levels

X_raw <- read_csv(
  "~/Documents/Research/Code/ECE/data/real-data/pce-components/pce_components_fredqd.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(sasdate = as.Date(sasdate, format = "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  arrange(sasdate)

X_mat_levels <- as.matrix(X_raw[, c("PCDGx", "PCNDx", "PCESVx")])
colnames(X_mat_levels) <- c("Durables", "Nondurables", "Services")
```

```{R pce-helpers}
#| echo: false

# Shared across both Raw and Log-Transformed below.

# Null-restricted z-test (rho = 0): avoids assuming Gaussian k40/k04/k31/k13,
# which the Kappa diagnostic tabs show are badly misspecified for this data.
ece_pval_null <- function(X) {
  p <- ncol(X)
  pval_mat <- matrix(NA, p, p)
  colnames(pval_mat) <- rownames(pval_mat) <- colnames(X)
  for (i in 1:(p - 1)) {
    for (j in (i + 1):p) {
      pair <- cbind(X[, i], X[, j])
      pval <- ece.test(pair, type = "z.test", kappa = ece.kappa(pair, rho = 0, method = "mom"), rho = 0)$p.value
      pval_mat[i, j] <- pval
      pval_mat[j, i] <- pval
    }
  }
  diag(pval_mat) <- 0
  pval_mat
}

# Bold any off-diagonal cell whose corresponding p-value is < 0.05.
bold_sig <- function(display_mat, pval_mat) {
  m   <- nrow(display_mat)
  out <- matrix("", m, m, dimnames = dimnames(display_mat))
  for (i in seq_len(m)) {
    for (j in seq_len(m)) {
      sig <- i != j && !is.na(pval_mat[i, j]) && pval_mat[i, j] < 0.05
      out[i, j] <- kableExtra::cell_spec(sprintf("%.3f", display_mat[i, j]), "html", bold = sig)
    }
  }
  out
}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Raw

We start with the raw dollar levels of the three PCE components — the same approach CPI Components uses successfully on price index levels. A hand-picked `pen.value` tuned for growth-rate scale over-segments badly here: it fits nearly every wiggle as a mean shift rather than genuine level changes, which pushes the pairwise ECE correlation outside the valid [-1, 1] range on the unsegmented data. `segment_mean(penalty = "BIC")` — the same automatic, data-driven criterion CPI Components uses on raw price-index levels — replaces that hand-tuned penalty below.

```{R pce-raw-load-data}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

X_mat_raw   <- X_mat_levels
X_seg_raw   <- segment_mean(X_mat_raw, penalty = "BIC")
X_resid_raw <- X_mat_raw - X_seg_raw

n_segs_raw <- apply(X_seg_raw, 2, function(c) length(unique(c)))
```

BIC finds `r n_segs_raw[["Durables"]]`, `r n_segs_raw[["Nondurables"]]`, and `r n_segs_raw[["Services"]]` segments for Durables, Nondurables, and Services respectively, out of `r nrow(X_mat_raw)` quarters.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Diagnostics

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Plot

```{R pce-raw-plot}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-pce-raw-bic
#| fig-cap: "Raw PCE component levels. Thick lines show the BIC-penalized segmented mean."

bind_cols(
  date = X_raw$sasdate,
  as.data.frame(X_mat_raw),
  as.data.frame(X_seg_raw) |> rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_segment"))
) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(
    type   = if_else(str_ends(series, "_segment"), "Segmented", "Raw"),
    sector = str_remove(series, "_segment$")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value, color = sector, group = series)) +
  geom_line(aes(linewidth = type)) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(Raw = 0.4, Segmented = 1.0), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~sector, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "PCE Component Levels (BIC Segmentation)", x = "Date", y = "Billions, chained dollars", color = "Component") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

BIC finds roughly a hundred segments per series over `r nrow(X_mat_raw)` quarters — coarser than a hand-tuned `pen.value = 0.005` (which fits nearly every quarter as its own segment), but still frequent relative to the handful of genuine recessions and shocks in this window.

#### Residuals

```{R pce-raw-residuals}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-pce-raw-bic-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residuals after removing the BIC-segmented mean from each raw-level component."

X_resid_raw |>
  as_tibble() |>
  bind_cols(date = X_raw$sasdate) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "sector", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value, color = sector)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~sector, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Residuals after BIC Segmentation (Raw Levels)", x = "Date", y = "Residual", color = "Component") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

#### ACF

::: {.panel-tabset}

##### Naive

```{R pce-raw-acf-naive}
#| echo: false

par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(0, 3, 0, 1), oma = c(4, 0, 1, 0), mgp = c(1.8, 1, 0))
for (i in 1:3) {
  acf(X_resid_raw[, i], main = "", xaxt = "n", ylab = colnames(X_resid_raw)[i])
}
axis(1)
mtext("Lag", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 2.5)
```

Lag-1 autocorrelation still sits around -0.5 to -0.6 for every series — the same order of magnitude a hand-tuned, over-segmenting penalty produces. BIC's coarser segment count doesn't fully resolve the negative-autocorrelation signature of over-fitting the mean; it's a real caveat on the raw-level results below, not a problem this penalty choice fixes outright.

##### Naive

##### Mean-Shift-Invariant

```{R pce-raw-trend-ece-data}
#| echo: false

window_raw <- max(10, floor(nrow(X_mat_raw) / 5))
cn_raw     <- colnames(X_mat_raw)
idx_raw    <- combn(ncol(X_mat_raw), 2)
n_raw      <- nrow(X_mat_raw)

ece_cov_raw <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx_raw)), function(k) {
  i <- idx_raw[1, k]
  j <- idx_raw[2, k]
  s <- lag_term(X_mat_raw[, i], X_mat_raw[, j])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n_raw), row = cn_raw[i], col = cn_raw[j], raw = s)
})
ece_var_raw <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(X_mat_raw)), function(i) {
  s <- lag_term(X_mat_raw[, i], X_mat_raw[, i])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n_raw), row = cn_raw[i], col = cn_raw[i], raw = s)
})
ece_terms_raw <- bind_rows(ece_cov_raw, ece_var_raw) |>
  mutate(row = factor(row, levels = cn_raw), col = factor(col, levels = cn_raw)) |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  mutate(run = rolling_mean(raw, window_raw), mean = mean(raw), median = median(raw)) |>
  ungroup()

ece_terms_raw_labels <- ece_terms_raw |> distinct(row, col, mean, median)
```

```{R pce-raw-trend-ece}
#| echo: false

ggplot(ece_terms_raw, aes(x = t)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = raw), color = "gray80") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean), linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = median), linetype = "dashed", color = "darkorange") +
  geom_line(aes(y = run), color = "steelblue", na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(row), cols = vars(col), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "time", y = "ECE term (covariance / variance scale)",
    subtitle = sprintf("gray = raw term, blue = %d-window mean, red = mean, orange = median", window_raw)
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{R pce-raw-trend-hist}
#| echo: false

ece_terms_raw_trimmed <- ece_terms_raw |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  filter(raw > quantile(raw, 0.005), raw < quantile(raw, 0.995)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(ece_terms_raw_trimmed, aes(x = raw)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(data = ece_terms_raw_labels, aes(xintercept = mean), color = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(data = ece_terms_raw_labels, aes(xintercept = median), color = "darkorange", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(row), cols = vars(col), scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "ECE term value (middle 99%)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Mean and median agree reasonably well in most panels, though not perfectly — consistent with the residual ACF above showing BIC's segmentation is a real improvement over a hand-tuned penalty, but not a fully clean fit.

:::

#### Kappa

```{R pce-raw-kappa-check}
#| echo: false

cn_raw_k  <- colnames(X_mat_raw)
idx_raw_k <- combn(ncol(X_mat_raw), 2)

kappa_tbl_raw <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx_raw_k)), function(k) {
  i <- idx_raw_k[1, k]
  j <- idx_raw_k[2, k]
  kap <- ece.kappa(X_resid_raw[, i], X_resid_raw[, j], method = "mom")
  tibble(
    Pair = paste(cn_raw_k[i], "/", cn_raw_k[j]),
    k40  = round(kap$k40, 2),
    k31  = round(kap$k31, 2),
    k22  = round(kap$k22, 2),
    k13  = round(kap$k13, 2),
    k04  = round(kap$k04, 2)
  )
})

kable(kappa_tbl_raw, align = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

Every term runs well past its Gaussian reference (`k40`, `k04` near 3; `k22` near 1), and several `k31`/`k13` terms come out negative — a well-behaved mean-zero residual shouldn't do that. As with Log-Transformed below, the Results section uses the null-restricted z-test (`rho = 0`) rather than assume the Gaussian reference values hold.

#### Omega

```{R pce-raw-omega-check}
#| echo: false

n_raw_o  <- nrow(X_mat_raw)
cn_raw_o <- colnames(X_mat_raw)

ece_omega_raw <- ece.complexity(X_mat_raw) |> round(6)
rownames(ece_omega_raw) <- colnames(ece_omega_raw) <- cn_raw_o

seg_omega_raw <- matrix(0, ncol(X_mat_raw), ncol(X_mat_raw), dimnames = list(cn_raw_o, cn_raw_o))
for (i in seq_len(ncol(X_mat_raw))) {
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(X_mat_raw))) {
    seg_omega_raw[i, j] <- lag_diff(X_seg_raw[, i], X_seg_raw[, j], k = 1) / n_raw_o
  }
}
seg_omega_raw <- round(seg_omega_raw, 6)
```

```{R pce-raw-omega-check-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(ece_omega_raw, caption = "ECE (raw levels, BIC segmentation)")
knitr::kable(seg_omega_raw, caption = "Segmentation-implied (raw levels, BIC)")
```

The two estimates agree to within 1-2% on every diagonal entry. As with CPI Components' raw-level check, that agreement is expected regardless of segmentation quality — raw dollar levels carry six decades of compounding growth, a mean-heterogeneity signal large enough that almost any reasonable segmentation captures its broad shape. It confirms the two methods see the same large trend; it doesn't by itself certify this particular BIC fit as correct, which is why the ACF tab's residual autocorrelation is the more informative diagnostic here.

:::

### Results

We start with pairwise comparisons: ECE and Segment-ECE — ECE applied to the raw levels and to the `segment_mean()` residuals — alongside naive and residual Pearson correlation, the same two versions of the data run through Pearson.

```{R pce-raw-pairwise-cor}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

ece_cor_raw               <- ece.cor(X_mat_raw) |> round(3)
rownames(ece_cor_raw)     <- colnames(ece_cor_raw) <- colnames(X_mat_raw)
seg_ece_cor_raw           <- ece.cor(X_resid_raw) |> round(3)
rownames(seg_ece_cor_raw) <- colnames(seg_ece_cor_raw) <- colnames(X_mat_raw)

resid_cor_raw   <- cor(X_resid_raw) |> round(3)
pearson_cor_raw <- cor(X_mat_raw) |> round(3)

ece_pmat_raw     <- ece_pval_null(X_mat_raw) |> round(3)
seg_ece_pmat_raw <- ece_pval_null(X_resid_raw) |> round(3)
resid_pmat_raw   <- cor_pval(X_resid_raw) |> round(3)
pearson_pmat_raw <- cor_pval(X_mat_raw) |> round(3)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Pairwise

::: {.panel-tabset}

##### Correlation

```{R pce-raw-pairwise-cor-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(bold_sig(ece_cor_raw, ece_pmat_raw),         caption = "ECE Correlation (Raw Levels, BIC)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(seg_ece_cor_raw, seg_ece_pmat_raw), caption = "Segment-ECE Correlation (Raw Levels, BIC)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(pearson_cor_raw, pearson_pmat_raw), caption = "Naive Pearson Correlation (Raw Levels)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(resid_cor_raw, resid_pmat_raw),     caption = "Residual Pearson Correlation (Raw Levels, BIC)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
```

Bold marks pairs significant at p < 0.05, using the same null-restricted z-test (`ece_pval_null()`) as the Log-Transformed Results section below.

##### P-Values

```{R pce-raw-pairwise-pval-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(bold_sig(ece_pmat_raw, ece_pmat_raw),         caption = "ECE P-Values, Raw Levels BIC (null-restricted z-test)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(seg_ece_pmat_raw, seg_ece_pmat_raw), caption = "Segment-ECE P-Values, Raw Levels BIC (null-restricted z-test)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(pearson_pmat_raw, pearson_pmat_raw), caption = "Naive Pearson P-Values, Raw Levels", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(resid_pmat_raw, resid_pmat_raw),     caption = "Residual Pearson P-Values, Raw Levels BIC", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
```

:::

Naive Pearson on the unsegmented levels runs 0.94-0.98 across all three pairs — every series shares the same six-decade growth trend, so this is almost entirely the shared-trend confound, not evidence of contemporaneous correlation. The pairwise ECE correlation on those same unsegmented levels comes out above 1 for the Durables/Services pair (1.349): the same `rotate()` boundary-wraparound failure mode CPI Components hits on its raw levels. Residualizing against the BIC segmentation fixes that — Segment-ECE stays within [-1, 1] for every pair (-0.070 to 0.169) — and residual Pearson collapses to near zero as well (-0.100 to 0.011). Under the null-restricted z-test, none of the three pairs reject on the residualized data (p = 0.051-0.654); the same is true of the unsegmented Segment-ECE-style comparison. This is the same qualitative picture as CPI Components' raw-level result — a shared trend, not real contemporaneous correlation — though the ACF tab's residual lag-1 autocorrelation (still around -0.5) means this reading carries more caveats here than CPI's cleaner BIC fit.

#### Diagonal

We run all four tests on the raw levels, then again on `X_resid_raw` — the same segmented residuals used for Segment-ECE above — as a check.

```{R pce-raw-diagonal-tests}
#| echo: false
set.seed(123)

results_raw <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Bootstrap Multiplier",
    "Parametric Bootstrap",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)",
    "Bartlett Test"
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    round(ece.test(X_mat_raw, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat_raw, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat_raw, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    round(cortest.bartlett(cor(X_mat_raw), nrow(X_mat_raw))$p.value, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

set.seed(123)
results_seg_raw <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Bootstrap Multiplier",
    "Parametric Bootstrap",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)",
    "Bartlett Test"
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    round(ece.test(X_resid_raw, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_resid_raw, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_resid_raw, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    round(cortest.bartlett(cor(X_resid_raw), nrow(X_resid_raw))$p.value, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

```{R pce-raw-diagonal-tests-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(results_raw,     caption = "Raw Levels (BIC), Unsegmented")
knitr::kable(results_seg_raw, caption = "Raw Levels (BIC), Segmented Residuals")
```

On the unsegmented levels (left), Bartlett and the naive parametric bootstrap both reject the diagonal null outright, while `bs.multiplier` and `bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd` fail to reject — the same split CPI Components finds on its own raw levels, and for the same reason: a shared trend fools the tests with no mean-shift mechanism, not the two that difference it away internally. Residualizing (right) brings all four tests to fail-to-reject, mirroring CPI's headline result. Given the ACF tab's residual autocorrelation, treat this agreement as directionally consistent with CPI Components rather than as clean as CPI's own BIC fit.

:::

:::

## Log-Transformed

Quarterly log growth rates, rather than dollar levels, are the standard economic convention for this kind of comparison — growth *rates* are the meaningful unit for spending, not dollar levels — and first-differencing fixes the segmentation problem the Raw section above works around by hand: a `pen.value` of 0.005 is the right order of magnitude for quarter-over-quarter growth rates.

```{R pce-load-data}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| label: pce-load-data

X_data <- X_raw |>
  mutate(
    Durables    = c(NA, diff(log(PCDGx))),
    Nondurables = c(NA, diff(log(PCNDx))),
    Services    = c(NA, diff(log(PCESVx))),
    Total       = c(NA, diff(log(PCECC96)))
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(Durables)) |>
  select(sasdate, Durables, Nondurables, Services, Total)

X_mat     <- as.matrix(X_data[, c("Durables", "Nondurables", "Services")])
X_segment <- segment_mean(X_mat, penalty = "Manual", pen.value = 0.005)
colnames(X_segment) <- colnames(X_mat)
X_resid   <- X_mat - X_segment

X <- bind_cols(date = X_data$sasdate, as.data.frame(X_mat), as.data.frame(X_segment) |> rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_segment")))
```

`r nrow(X_data)` quarterly growth-rate observations. Every diagnostic below flags the same single quarter — 2020-06-01, the COVID lockdown shock — as an extreme outlier dominating the term distribution (Trend tab) and the excess kurtosis in every pair's Kappa estimate, especially those touching `Services`. The two tabs below check how much of this chapter's conclusions depend on the pandemic era: `Full Sample` is the analysis above in its usual form, `Pre-COVID` reruns the identical pipeline restricted to `sasdate < 2020-01-01` — dropping the pandemic shock itself and every quarter since, not just the single worst one.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Full Sample

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Diagnostics

::: {.panel-tabset}

##### Plot

```{R pce-plot-raw}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-pce-growth
#| fig-cap: "Quarterly log growth rates by PCE component. Thick lines show segmented means."

X |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(
    type   = if_else(str_ends(series, "_segment"), "Segmented", "Raw"),
    sector = str_remove(series, "_segment$")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value, color = sector, group = series)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray") +
  geom_line(aes(linewidth = type)) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(Raw = 0.4, Segmented = 1.0), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~sector, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "PCE Growth by Component",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Log Growth Rate",
    color = "Component",
    caption = "Source: FRED-QD (McCracken-Ng)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Durables is the most volatile series and picks up the most breakpoints — recessions in 1971, 1973-75, 1980, and 2008-09 each register as a distinct segment, on top of the 2020 spike. Nondurables finds no breaks at all at this penalty. Services stays essentially flat except for a single, massive segment around the 2020 lockdowns.

##### Residuals

```{R pce-plot-residuals}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-pce-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residuals after removing the segmented mean from each component."

X_resid |>
  as_tibble() |>
  bind_cols(date = X_data$sasdate) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "sector", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value, color = sector)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~sector, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals after Segmentation",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Residual",
    color = "Component"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Nondurables' "residual" is just its mean-centered raw series, since no segments were found. The 2020 spike dominates Services even after segmentation removes its own dedicated segment mean — the shock itself was more of an outlier than a shift in level.

##### ACF

::: {.panel-tabset}

###### Naive

```{R pce-acf-naive}
#| echo: false

par(mfrow = c(ncol(X_resid), 1), mar = c(0, 3, 0, 1), oma = c(4, 0, 1, 0), mgp = c(1.8, 1, 0))

for (i in seq_len(ncol(X_resid))) {
  acf(X_resid[, i], main = "", xaxt = "n", ylab = colnames(X_resid)[i])
}
axis(1)
mtext("Lag", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 2.5)
```

All three residual series sit close to zero autocorrelation at every lag — the cleanest ACF diagnostic of any real-data chapter in this book. Quarterly consumption growth just doesn't carry much quarter-to-quarter momentum once its own mean is accounted for.

###### Mean-Shift-Invariant

```{R pce-trend-ece-data}
#| echo: false

cn     <- colnames(X_mat)
idx    <- combn(ncol(X_mat), 2)
n      <- nrow(X_mat)
window <- max(10, floor(n / 5))

ece_cov_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx)), function(k) {
  i <- idx[1, k]
  j <- idx[2, k]
  s <- lag_term(X_mat[, i], X_mat[, j])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[j], raw = s)
})
ece_var_dat <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(X_mat)), function(i) {
  s <- lag_term(X_mat[, i], X_mat[, i])
  tibble(t = seq_len(n), row = cn[i], col = cn[i], raw = s)
})
ece_terms_dat <- bind_rows(ece_cov_dat, ece_var_dat) |>
  mutate(row = factor(row, levels = cn), col = factor(col, levels = cn)) |>

  mutate(run = rolling_mean(raw, window), mean = mean(raw), median = median(raw)) |>

ece_terms_labels <- ece_terms_dat |> distinct(row, col, mean, median)
```

```{R pce-trend-ece}
  labs(

  ) +

```

Every panel's largest single term value falls at the same quarter: 2020-06-01, the COVID lockdown shock. Same 3x3 layout as the histogram below (diagonal = variance term, upper triangle = covariance term), so both diagnose the same panels directly against each other.

```{R pce-trend-hist}
#| echo: false

ece_terms_summary <- ece_terms_dat |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(raw), median = median(raw), .groups = "drop")

ece_terms_trimmed <- ece_terms_dat |>
  group_by(row, col) |>
  filter(raw > quantile(raw, 0.005), raw < quantile(raw, 0.995)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(ece_terms_trimmed, aes(x = raw)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(data = ece_terms_summary, aes(xintercept = mean), color = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(data = ece_terms_summary, aes(xintercept = median), color = "darkorange", linetype = "dashed") +

```

Almost every observation sits in a single bar near zero. The mean (dashed red) sits visibly to the right of the median (dashed orange) in every panel — the 2020-06-01 term alone is large enough to pull the mean well off the bulk of the distribution, even trimmed to the middle 99%. That single quarter is exactly what the Kappa tab below flags as driving excess kurtosis in every pair, especially those involving `Services`.

:::

##### Kappa

The default pairwise z-test (`ece.test(..., type = "z.test")`) uses `kappa = "gaussian"`: a delta-method standard error that assumes the fourth-moment terms take their Gaussian values (`k40 = k04 = 3`, `k22 = 1 + 2ρ²`, `k31 = k13 = 3ρ`). We check that assumption directly, estimating these terms from the segmented residuals (`ece.kappa(..., method = "mom")`):

```{R pce-kappa-check}
#| echo: false

cn  <- colnames(X_mat)
idx <- combn(ncol(X_mat), 2)

kappa_tbl <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx)), function(k) {
  i <- idx[1, k]
  j <- idx[2, k]
  kap <- ece.kappa(X_resid[, i], X_resid[, j], method = "mom")
  tibble(
    Pair = paste(cn[i], "/", cn[j]),
    k40  = round(kap$k40, 2),
    k31  = round(kap$k31, 2),
    k22  = round(kap$k22, 2),
    k13  = round(kap$k13, 2),
    k04  = round(kap$k04, 2)
  )
})

kable(kappa_tbl, align = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

Every estimate here runs well above the Gaussian reference (`k40`, `k04` near 3; `k22` near 1). `Nondurables/Services` is the most extreme, with `k40` = 31.69, `k22` = 44.61, `k04` = 83.11. `Services`' own marginal term (`k04`, last two rows) reaches 83.11 — consistent with the Trend tab's histogram, where a single quarter (2020-06-01) sits far outside the bulk of every distribution `Services` participates in. The `kappa = "gaussian"` z-test understates the true standard error for these pairs. See the `Pre-COVID` tab: restricting to data before 2020 brings every one of these terms back near its Gaussian reference, so the pandemic era — not just the single worst quarter — is what's driving this misspecification.

**Fix: test under the null instead of estimating all five kappas.** `ece.cor.se()` forces `ρ = 0` when `rho = 0` is passed. Every kappa term with a nonzero coefficient in the SE formula — `k40`, `k04`, `k31`, `k13` — carries a factor of `ρ` or `ρ²`, so at `ρ = 0` they all drop out algebraically. Only `k22` remains, and under true independence it collapses to exactly 1 for any marginal distribution, not just Gaussian. The Results section below uses this null-restricted z-test — `kappa = ece.kappa(X, rho = 0, method = "mom")`, `rho = 0` — for both `ECE` and `Segment-ECE`, instead of the full Gaussian one.

##### Omega

This chapter residualizes with `segment_mean(penalty = "Manual", pen.value = 0.005)`, a penalty chosen by eye to recover economically sensible breakpoints — not a principled fit like the Raw section's BIC penalty above. We check it against ECE's own segmentation-free estimate of $\omega$, the mean-heterogeneity parameter from `omega-estimation.qmd`. `ece.complexity()` estimates $\omega$ directly from the raw data via lagged differences. If the hand-tuned segmentation describes the data well, the same $\omega$ quantity computed from the fitted segmented mean should closely match it.

```{R pce-omega-check}
#| echo: false

n  <- nrow(X_mat)
cn <- colnames(X_mat)

ece_omega <- ece.complexity(X_mat) |> round(6)
rownames(ece_omega) <- colnames(ece_omega) <- cn

seg_omega <- matrix(0, ncol(X_mat), ncol(X_mat), dimnames = list(cn, cn))
for (i in seq_len(ncol(X_mat))) {
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(X_mat))) {
    seg_omega[i, j] <- lag_diff(X_segment[, i], X_segment[, j], k = 1) / n
  }
}
seg_omega <- round(seg_omega, 6)
```

```{R pce-omega-check-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(ece_omega, caption = "ECE (raw data, no segmentation)")
knitr::kable(seg_omega, caption = "Segmentation-implied")
```

Unlike the Raw section above, where the two estimates agreed to within 1-2%, they disagree here — in sign as well as magnitude. ECE's own estimate is negative everywhere, including on the diagonal; the segmentation-implied version is positive wherever it found a break (`Durables`, `Services`) and exactly zero wherever it didn't (`Nondurables`, which found no segments at all — see the Plot tab). Both sets of numbers are small: on the order of 1e-4 to 1e-6, next to values in the tens of thousands for the Raw section's dollar-level $\omega$. That scale difference is the more informative signal. Raw dollar levels carry six decades of compounding growth, a mean-heterogeneity signal orders of magnitude larger than anything in this chapter's already-differenced growth rates. There simply isn't much mean-shift structure left to detect here, which is consistent with this chapter's near-zero ACF (see the ACF tab) and casts the hand-picked `pen.value = 0.005` breakpoints as a reasonable read of a mostly-flat mean process, not a confirmed one.

:::

#### Results

Beyond the pairwise correlations, we can test the joint null hypothesis that the full 3x3 correlation matrix is diagonal — i.e. that none of the three PCE components are contemporaneously correlated.

```{R pce-calc-cor}
#| echo: false

ece_cor               <- ece.cor(X_mat) |> round(3)
rownames(ece_cor)     <- colnames(ece_cor) <- colnames(X_mat)
seg_ece_cor           <- ece.cor(X_resid) |> round(3)
rownames(seg_ece_cor) <- colnames(seg_ece_cor) <- colnames(X_mat)

resid_cor   <- cor(X_resid) |> round(3)
pearson_cor <- cor(X_mat) |> round(3)

ece_pmat     <- ece_pval_null(X_mat) |> round(3)
seg_ece_pmat <- ece_pval_null(X_resid) |> round(3)
resid_pmat   <- cor_pval(X_resid) |> round(3)
pearson_pmat <- cor_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

##### Pairwise

::: {.panel-tabset}

###### Correlation

```{R pce-output-cor}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(bold_sig(ece_cor, ece_pmat),         caption = "ECE Correlation", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(seg_ece_cor, seg_ece_pmat), caption = "Segment-ECE Correlation", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(pearson_cor, pearson_pmat), caption = "Naive Pearson Correlation", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(resid_cor, resid_pmat),     caption = "Residual Pearson Correlation", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
```

###### P-Values

```{R pce-output-pval}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(bold_sig(ece_pmat, ece_pmat),         caption = "ECE P-Values (null-restricted z-test)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(seg_ece_pmat, seg_ece_pmat), caption = "Segment-ECE P-Values (null-restricted z-test)", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(pearson_pmat, pearson_pmat), caption = "Naive Pearson P-Values", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
knitr::kable(bold_sig(resid_pmat, resid_pmat),     caption = "Residual Pearson P-Values", escape = FALSE, format = "html")
```

:::

Bold marks pairs significant at p < 0.05: correlation cells bold when the matching p-value clears it, p-value cells bold when they clear it themselves.

Naive Pearson puts Durables-Nondurables at 0.478 and Nondurables-Services at 0.539, both significant. Residualizing pulls Durables-Nondurables down to 0.310 (still significant, p = 0.022) and Nondurables-Services to 0.579 (still significant). ECE (raw) and Segment-ECE go further on that same pair — 0.745 and 0.720 — well above either Pearson version, for the reason the Omega tab traces to `Nondurables` carrying no detected mean shift into every comparison it's part of, unlike its partners. See the `Pre-COVID` tab: restricted to data before 2020, ECE for this pair drops to 0.209/0.207 — well below even naive Pearson — and no pair reaches p < 0.05 under the null-restricted z-test at all. The full-sample significance on Durables-Nondurables doesn't survive dropping the pandemic era.

But under the null-restricted z-test (Kappa tab), only Durables-Nondurables clears p < 0.05 for both ECE (p = 0.043) and Segment-ECE (p = 0.038). Durables-Services and Nondurables-Services — the two pairs involving `Services`, whose residuals carry the heaviest excess kurtosis in the Kappa table — don't reject under either ECE variant (p = 0.127-0.183), despite Pearson finding both significant on the same data. The two families of test agree on which pair is strongest and disagree on whether the other two are distinguishable from noise, and the disagreement traces directly to the kappa misspecification diagnosed above, not to a different point estimate.

##### Diagonal

We run all four tests on the raw growth rates, then again on `X_resid` — the same segmented residuals used for Segment-ECE above — as a check.

```{R pce-diagonal-tests}
#| echo: false
set.seed(123)

results <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Bootstrap Multiplier",
    "Parametric Bootstrap",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)",
    "Bartlett Test"
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    round(ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    round(cortest.bartlett(cor(X_mat), nrow(X_mat))$p.value, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

set.seed(123)
results_seg <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Bootstrap Multiplier",
    "Parametric Bootstrap",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)",
    "Bartlett Test"
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    round(ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    round(cortest.bartlett(cor(X_resid), nrow(X_resid))$p.value, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

```{R pce-diagonal-tests-output}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(results,     caption = "Raw Growth Rates")
knitr::kable(results_seg, caption = "Segmented Residuals")
```

On the raw growth rates (left), the tests split. Bartlett and the naive parametric bootstrap both reject the diagonal null outright — expected, since all three components share the same consumer spending cycle. But the two tests built on ECE's default lag-1 block difference (`bs.multiplier`, `bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd`) don't reject at conventional levels. With near-zero autocorrelation in every series (see the ACF tab), there's no leftover momentum to blame this time, unlike the Raw section's rejections above, which carry a real residual-autocorrelation caveat.

Removing the segmented mean (right) barely moves any of the four p-values: 0.281 to 0.261, 0.401 to 0.264, 0.004 to 0.008, and Bartlett stays at essentially 0. That's a different outcome than the Raw section above, where residualizing brought all four tests to fail-to-reject. Here Bartlett keeps rejecting even after the mean shift is removed by hand — consistent with the Omega tab's finding that this data doesn't carry much mean-heterogeneity to begin with, and with the pairwise correlations above, where two of three pairs stay significant under residualized Pearson. The split between the two ECE bootstrap variants and everything else isn't a mean-shift artifact here; it's a genuine disagreement in how the four tests treat the same, already fairly stationary data. See the `Pre-COVID` tab: `bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd` moves noticeably closer to rejection (0.081-0.100) once the pandemic era is dropped entirely, though `bs.multiplier` stays comfortably non-significant — the split narrows on one bootstrap variant but not the other.

:::

:::

### Pre-COVID

Same pipeline as `Full Sample`, restricted to `sasdate < 2020-01-01` — everything from the pandemic quarter onward dropped, not just 2020-06-01 itself.

```{R pce-pre-load-data}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

X_data_pre <- X_data |> filter(sasdate < as.Date("2020-01-01"))
X_mat_pre  <- as.matrix(X_data_pre[, c("Durables", "Nondurables", "Services")])
dates_pre  <- X_data_pre$sasdate

X_segment_pre <- segment_mean(X_mat_pre, penalty = "Manual", pen.value = 0.005)
colnames(X_segment_pre) <- colnames(X_mat_pre)
X_resid_pre <- X_mat_pre - X_segment_pre

n_segs_pre <- apply(X_segment_pre, 2, function(c) length(unique(c)))
```

`r nrow(X_data_pre)` observations instead of `r nrow(X_data)`, ending `r format(max(X_data_pre$sasdate))`. Durables still finds `r n_segs_pre[["Durables"]]` segments; Nondurables and Services both drop to a single segment (`r n_segs_pre[["Nondurables"]]`, `r n_segs_pre[["Services"]]`) — Services' entire 2020-tied segment disappears along with the window that produced it.

::: {.panel-tabset}

##### Kappa

```{R pce-pre-kappa-check}
#| echo: false

cn_pre  <- colnames(X_mat_pre)
idx_pre <- combn(ncol(X_mat_pre), 2)

kappa_tbl_pre <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx_pre)), function(k) {
  i <- idx_pre[1, k]
  j <- idx_pre[2, k]
  kap <- ece.kappa(X_resid_pre[, i], X_resid_pre[, j], method = "mom")
  tibble(
    Pair = paste(cn_pre[i], "/", cn_pre[j]),
    k40  = round(kap$k40, 2),
    k31  = round(kap$k31, 2),
    k22  = round(kap$k22, 2),
    k13  = round(kap$k13, 2),
    k04  = round(kap$k04, 2)
  )
})

kable(kappa_tbl_pre, align = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

This is the answer to whether COVID was driving the Kappa misspecification: yes, but only the whole pandemic-and-after window, not the single worst quarter. Every term here sits close to its Gaussian reference (`k40`/`k04` 4.6-6.4 against 3, `k22` 1.1-1.4 against 1, `k31`/`k13` near 0) — a dramatic contrast with the Full Sample tab's `k04` up to 83.11 and `k22` up to 44.61. `Services`' heavy tails, which looked structural when only 2020-06-01 was dropped, turn out to be concentrated in 2020 and after; restricted to the years before the pandemic, `Services` behaves close to Gaussian like its partners.

##### Omega

```{R pce-pre-omega-check}

rownames(ece_omega_pre) <- colnames(ece_omega_pre) <- cn_pre_o

for (i in seq_len(ncol(X_mat_pre))) {
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(X_mat_pre))) {
    seg_omega_pre[i, j] <- lag_diff(X_segment_pre[, i], X_segment_pre[, j], k = 1) / n_pre
  }
}
seg_omega_pre <- round(seg_omega_pre, 6)

knitr::kable(ece_omega_pre, caption = "ECE (log growth, pre-COVID)")
knitr::kable(seg_omega_pre, caption = "Segmentation-implied (pre-COVID)")
```

Both estimates shrink further than in the Full Sample tab — unsurprising, since the pandemic era supplied the largest terms in every panel of that tab's Trend diagnostic. The two still disagree in sign, same as the Full Sample tab: whatever mean-heterogeneity this dataset carries, it's small before 2020 too.

##### Diagonal

```{R pce-pre-diagonal}
#| echo: false
set.seed(123)

results_pre <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Bootstrap Multiplier", "Parametric Bootstrap", "Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)", "Bartlett Test"),
  `p-value` = c(
    round(ece.test(X_mat_pre, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat_pre, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_mat_pre, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    round(cortest.bartlett(cor(X_mat_pre), nrow(X_mat_pre))$p.value, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

set.seed(123)
results_seg_pre <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Bootstrap Multiplier", "Parametric Bootstrap", "Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)", "Bartlett Test"),
  `p-value` = c(
    round(ece.test(X_resid_pre, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_resid_pre, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value, 3),
    round(ece.test(X_resid_pre, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value, 3),
    round(cortest.bartlett(cor(X_resid_pre), nrow(X_resid_pre))$p.value, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(results_pre,     caption = "Raw Growth Rates (Pre-COVID)")
knitr::kable(results_seg_pre, caption = "Segmented Residuals (Pre-COVID)")
```

Bartlett and the naive bootstrap still reject outright (both essentially 0), same as the Full Sample tab. `bs.multiplier` stays comfortably non-significant (0.212/0.168, close to the full sample's 0.281/0.261). `bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd` moves the most: 0.081 unsegmented, 0.100 residualized — right at the conventional boundary, down from 0.401/0.264 in the full sample. The two ECE-based bootstraps no longer agree with each other as clearly as they did on the full sample: one stays solidly non-significant, the other sits on the fence. That's a real, if partial, erosion of the "ECE-based tests cleanly fail to reject" reading once the pandemic era — not just its single worst quarter — is removed.

:::

:::

:::

:::

Where this leaves us: naive Pearson correlation finds all three PCE components significantly related, unsurprising since they're accounting components of the same aggregate. Removing the mean shift changes the story more for some pairs than others — Durables-Nondurables weakens under both residualized Pearson and ECE, while Nondurables-Services strengthens sharply under ECE specifically (0.539 naive to 0.745), driven by Nondurables carrying no detected mean shift into the comparison at all — a finding the Omega tab independently corroborates, since this dataset's mean-heterogeneity is small enough that ECE's own segmentation-free estimate and the hand-tuned `segment_mean()` fit disagree even in sign.

Whether that gap counts as "real" depends on which z-test you trust — and on which years you trust it on. The Kappa tab shows the default Gaussian z-test is badly misspecified on the full sample — every pair's fourth-moment terms run 2x to 30x their Gaussian reference. The `Pre-COVID` tab traces that misspecification to the pandemic era specifically, not to any single quarter: restricted to `sasdate < 2020-01-01`, every kappa term sits close to its Gaussian reference, and the one pairwise result that survived the full sample's null-restricted z-test (Durables-Nondurables, p = 0.043/0.038) no longer clears p < 0.05 once that era is excluded (p = 0.099/0.095). Naive Pearson and Bartlett can't see any of this — a reminder that "significant under Pearson" and "significant under a z-test calibrated to this data's actual moments, in this particular window" are different claims, not just different point estimates.

The joint-diagonal tests split along a different line on the full sample: Bartlett and the naive bootstrap reject on both raw and residualized data, ECE's own lag-1-block-based bootstraps don't reject either version. Unlike the Raw section above, residualizing doesn't resolve this split on the log-transformed side, because there was little mean shift for it to remove in the first place. The `Pre-COVID` tab shows this split narrowing on one of the two ECE-based tests, not both: `bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd` moves to the conventional boundary (0.081-0.100) once the pandemic era is dropped, while `bs.multiplier` stays comfortably non-significant throughout, and Bartlett/naive bootstrap keep rejecting regardless of window. That's evidence the full-sample non-rejection was, for one of the two ECE-based tests, partly propped up by the pandemic era's outsized weight in its construction — not evidence the pandemic was a contaminant every other test correctly ignored, since Bartlett and naive bootstrap reject in both windows. The Raw section's own residualized results (all four tests fail to reject) are directionally consistent with the log-transformed full-sample picture, but come with the ACF caveat noted there — the two sections agree on the qualitative picture more than they agree cleanly on every number.
